The [previous article](/posts/the-agent-is-the-easy-part/index.qmd) built AnswerTrail: a research agent that answers questions from one YouTube creator's transcripts, with every citation checked against the corpus.
This article asks whether it is any good, and the honest answer needs a measuring instrument built as carefully as the agent.

The headline is a gap.
The agent answers single-fact questions well and change-over-time questions poorly, 87 percent against 32 percent.
The interesting part is why, and the finding is that the gap is dominantly a retrieval problem.
For the hard questions, the evidence an answer needs is usually never retrieved in the first place.
Getting to that claim, and being able to trust it, took two things: a gold standard that says what each answer must contain, and a judge whose verdicts have been checked against a human.
This article builds both, then reports what the agent scores.

## What we measure against is nuggets

Measurement starts from gold data: for each question, the set of facts a correct answer must state.
AnswerTrail is evaluated on two kinds of question.
A **factual question** asks for one specific fact.
A **longitudinal question** asks how the creator's view on a topic changed over time.

Each evaluation example is a question paired with a set of nuggets.
A **nugget** is one atomic fact a correct answer must state, and it is the unit recall is scored against.
A factual nugget is a single fact; a longitudinal nugget is a stance plus a time window.

Nuggets are not written from scratch.
They are extracted from claims, and claims are extracted from chunks, so three units stack up:

- A **chunk** is a fixed 30-second transcript window, the atomic unit the agent searches and cites. Its id is `video_id:start_second`.
- A **claim** is one atomic, faithful assertion a video makes, extracted from the transcript and tied to the chunk or chunks that state it. Its id is `video_id#cNNN`, and the extractor also attaches short topic and entity tags.
- A **nugget** is one atomic fact a correct answer must state.

## From chunks to claims

Claims are the shared raw material for both question tiers, so they are built first.
For each video, the pipeline loads the video's chunks in start-time order, renders them as a numbered list, and calls Sonnet 5 with thinking off and a claim-extraction prompt.
A single call produces, for each claim, its text, the chunk indices that support it, and its topic and entity tags.

```
Extract EVERY concrete claim, finding, number, result, comparison, or stated opinion...
For each claim, list in evidence_indices the indices of the chunk(s) that support it.
Never cite a chunk that does not state the claim.
```

A human review of a first extraction pass over 3 sample videos caught over-extraction, where production narration and blow-by-blow demo transcripts were being turned into claims.
That drove one prompt revision, which took those 3 videos from 210 claims to 145 before the full pass ran over the whole corpus.
A real extracted claim, with the tags produced in the same call:

```json
{ "claim_id": "-HjPWrKavyA#c016",
  "text":     "Claude 4.5 scored 77% on general finance in this study.",
  "chunk_ids":["-HjPWrKavyA:00390", "-HjPWrKavyA:00420"],
  "topics":   ["FIRE benchmark", "model comparison"],
  "entities": ["Claude 4.5"],
  "confidence":"high" }
```

Over the corpus this yields 26,240 claims, a median of 54 per video.

## Factual gold: 25 questions, 53 nuggets

The factual tier asks for a single specific fact, so its gold is a small set of atomic facts per question, produced in four steps.

**Sample over time, not topic.**
Order the 475 videos by date, divide them into 5 equal-count bins of about 95 videos each, and take a seeded draw of 10 videos from each.
The 50 source videos then span the whole 16-month range rather than clustering on the creator's most prolific months.

**Select and compose, two calls per video.**
A cheap thinking-off Sonnet 5 call picks the video's 2 most question-worthy high-confidence claims, and the script keeps one as primary and one as fallback.
An adaptive-thinking call then writes one natural question from the primary claim, anchored to at least one identifying specific and careful never to include the part of the claim the question is asking for.
The output is 50 question candidates, one per sampled video, each paired with its source claim.

**Human adjudication.**
Not every composed question is usable, so a human vets each one with its claim and chunks, and 26 of the 50 survive.
The common reasons for cutting a question are that it already contained its own answer, or that it read like something no real user would type, for example: *"In a paper's worked example on agent matchmaking with a pool of 100 agents, cosine similarity is used to match agent self-descriptions to subtasks - which agent was identified as the best fit for subtask one, and what was its similarity score?"*

**Nugget extraction.**
For each surviving question, a Sonnet 5 call decomposes its claim into the atomic facts an answer must state, while omitting anything already given in the question.

```
question : Which universities published ReasonFlux, and when did the paper come out?
claim    : The creator states that Princeton University and Peking University already
           implemented this exact approach, publishing it on February 10th, 2025,
           calling it ReasonFlux.
nuggets  : fc-0001_n1  "ReasonFlux was published by Princeton University."
           fc-0001_n2  "ReasonFlux was published by Peking University."
           fc-0001_n3  "ReasonFlux was published on February 10th, 2025."
```

The first automated run produced 69 nuggets across the 26 questions.
Manual adjudication then removed nuggets that described properties already stated in the question, leaving 25 questions with 53 nuggets.

## Longitudinal gold: 35 questions

The longitudinal tier draws on the same claims but asks a harder question.
A longitudinal question is about how the creator's view on a topic changed over time, and that kind of change never shows up in a single claim.
So the gold is built from a topic's claims tracked over time, again in four steps.

**Build threads.**
A **thread** groups high-confidence claims that share a normalized topic tag, keeping only groups that span at least 3 videos and at least 90 days, ordered by date.
Normalizing a tag is purely lexical: lowercase it, drop parenthetical asides, turn hyphens into spaces, and strip a trailing role word, so "In-Context Learning" and "in context learning" both become `in context learning`.
The intuition is that three videos means the topic is not a one-off, and ninety days means enough time for a view to actually change.
A stop-list drops generic non-trajectory topics first (`benchmarks`, `model comparison`, `methodology`, `publication date`, and so on).
A real thread, abbreviated, is the `reinforcement learning` thread, a family of 134 videos and 301 dated claims spanning 461 days:

```
### topic:reinforcement learning  [videos=134, span=461d, claims=301]  2025-01-10 -> 2026-04-16
  2025-01-10 [FR8oE8chp7c#c019] new data or RL approaches do not override the root-cause reasoning engine's outdated knowledge
  2025-01-29 [2ENvGkkK36E#c002] DeepSeek's R1 paper explains GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) in detail
  2025-02-02 [bjktcqGxxac#c039] RL-tuned models like o1 and R1 are optimized for final-answer correctness, not reasoning
  ... (+298 more claims)
```

**Compose a question from each thread.**
Each thread goes to one adaptive-thinking Sonnet 5 call whose input is the dated claims and whose output is three things at once: a question, a `trajectory_must_say` of 2 to 4 arc statements describing how the view changed, and 3 to 6 of the thread's claims chosen as dated evidence.
The claims are not generated here; they are the thread's existing claims that the call selects.
Before it composes any of that, the same call applies a development test: it must first decide whether the thread shows genuine development, and reject threads that merely restate the same point over time.
Of about 1,105 threads left after the stop-list, 505 pass this test.

**Triage arcs versus collections.**
Passing the development test is necessary but not sufficient, because Sonnet 5 cannot reliably separate two things.
An **arc** is a genuine trajectory: the creator's own position, or his own test's results, moving directionally on one object over time.
A **collection** is separate points that merely share a topic word, like several facts about RAG across the year with no single evolving position; it looks longitudinal but is really a list.
A human reads all 505 questions with their arc statements, and after keeping only the genuine trajectories, 35 questions remain.

**Extract nuggets from arcs.**
Not every fact in a thread becomes a nugget.
Because the corpus is large, there are many plausible routes from a starting stance to an ending stance, so two correct answers can tell the same story through different intermediate points.
A nugget should therefore capture only the route-independent parts of the arc: the starting stance, each genuine turning point, the ending stance, and the change itself.
The test for each candidate nugget is answerable yes or no: could a correct answer, taking a different route through the corpus, omit this and still tell the same story?
If yes, it is supporting evidence, not a nugget; if no, it is a nugget.

There is one nugget every longitudinal question carries that the stance nuggets cannot replace.
The stance nuggets can each be satisfied on their own: "in early 2025 he was optimistic," "in mid-2025 he tempered," "in early 2026 he concluded it had stalled."
An answer can hit all three and still describe them as three disconnected snapshots, never saying that the optimism became the tempering became the conclusion.
So each question also carries one **shift nugget**, graded as a connection, which asks whether the answer asserts the trajectory itself rather than just enumerating its points:

```
n1 (stance) He was optimistic about agentic AI's real-world capability and near-term
            impact [early 2025]
n2 (stance) He tempered that view: on realistic evaluation, agentic performance was
            weak [mid 2025]
n3 (stance) He concluded the anticipated agentic-AI revolution had stalled [early 2026]
n4 (shift)  He moved from early-2025 optimism, through a mid-2025 tempering, to an
            early-2026 conclusion that the promised agentic revolution had stalled
            [Feb 2025 - Jan 2026]
```

## One judge, pointed three ways

With the gold built, the question is how the frozen agent scores against it.
Scoring uses a single LLM judge that runs on a different model family, Claude Sonnet 5, from the OpenAI `gpt-5.4` agent it grades, so the system never grades its own output.
The judge always does the same thing: given a claim and a piece of text, it decides HIT or MISS on whether the text supports the claim.

```
You decide whether a single CLAIM is supported by a given TEXT. Output a binary
verdict - HIT or MISS - and a one-sentence reason. There is no middle category...
Be strict about substance and lenient about wording. Do not reward a text that is
merely on the same topic; require that it actually supports the specific claim.
```

The three checks differ only in what the claim and the text are:

- **Recall** checks a gold nugget against the agent's answer: does the answer contain each nugget it should?
- **Groundedness** checks an answer claim against the retrieved chunks: is each thing the agent asserted actually backed by what it retrieved?
- **Retrieval** checks a gold nugget against the retrieved chunks: was the nugget's evidence even retrieved? The share of nuggets where it was is the **retrieval ceiling**, the highest recall the agent could reach given what retrieval surfaced.

Recall and retrieval hand the judge its two texts directly.
Groundedness needs one extra step first: an LLM call extracts the atomic claims the agent's answer makes, and each of those is then checked against the retrieved chunks.
That extractor is told to pull the individual period stances an answer makes, and specifically not to extract a cross-video shift or trajectory statement, so groundedness is scored on checkable assertions.

## Can we trust the judge?

Every number rests on the judge's verdicts, and an LLM judge is itself a fallible model, so before relying on it we calibrate it against a human.
We draw 66 pairs and hand each to both the judge and a human, who each say HIT or MISS on whether the claim is supported by the text.

The pairs cover all three checks.
Each check needs both clear hits and clear misses, and groundedness is almost always a hit, so we add a few constructed misses: one of the agent's own claims paired with the chunks retrieved for a different, unrelated question, which cannot support it.
The human labels all 66 blind, seeing only each claim and its text, with the judge's verdict and reasoning hidden.
Across the 66 pairs the judge called 36 hits and 30 misses, while the human labeled 32 hits and 34 misses.

The calibration score is how often the two agree, corrected for the agreement you would expect by chance.
That chance-corrected measure is Cohen's kappa, where $p_o$ is the observed agreement and $p_e$ the agreement expected if each labeled at its own hit and miss rate:

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

The observed agreement is $p_o = 62/66 = 0.9394$, and the chance agreement from the two distributions is $p_e = \frac{36}{66}\cdot\frac{32}{66} + \frac{30}{66}\cdot\frac{34}{66} = 0.4986$, giving:

$$\kappa = \frac{0.9394 - 0.4986}{1 - 0.4986} = 0.879$$

A kappa of 0.879 is high agreement, so the scores below reflect the agent's behavior rather than the judge's quirks.

## The results

The main study is simple to state: run the frozen agent over every gold question and score each answer.
The agent (`gpt-5.4`, reasoning effort low, dense pgvector retrieval, top-10 per search, up to 15 steps) answered each of the 25 factual and 35 longitudinal questions three times.

| Metric | Factual | Longitudinal |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| Recall | 86.9% | 32.2% |
| Groundedness | 96.0% | 97.9% |
| Retrieval ceiling | 86.8% | 43.5% |

The two tiers even work differently.
A factual run took about 5 reasoning loops and about 4 searches, and surfaced about 19 chunks for synthesis.
A longitudinal run worked harder, about 7 loops and about 9 searches, often firing several searches in one loop, and surfaced about 40 chunks.

Longitudinal questions are inherently harder.
A factual answer needs a single fact from usually one place, whereas a longitudinal answer must gather and connect evidence scattered across many videos and many months.

The scores locate where that difficulty bites.
The gap is dominantly retrieval: the retrieval ceiling, the fraction of gold nuggets whose evidence was retrieved at all, is only 43.5% for longitudinal against 86.8% for factual.
Groundedness stays high on both tiers, 96 to 98%, so almost everything the agent asserts is backed by the chunks it actually retrieved.
The agent is not making things up and it is not reasoning badly over what it has.
It simply never sees the evidence for more than half of what a trajectory answer must say.

## What would move it

With a judge we can trust, we can price the two obvious levers: a better retriever, and no agent loop at all.

**A better ranker does not help.**
A pre-registered ablation on the longitudinal questions swapped dense retrieval for hybrid retrieval (dense plus BM25, fused with reciprocal rank fusion), to test whether a stronger ranker raises the ceiling.
The single hybrid run came out essentially identical to the three-run dense baseline: a retrieval ceiling of 40.2% against 43.5%, and recall of 31.1% against 32.2%.

**The loop buys coverage.**
The other ablation removes the ReAct loop entirely, running one dense retrieval on the raw question and then one synthesis call with no exploration.
On factual questions, plain RAG scores 82.0% recall against the agent's 86.9%, so the loop adds 4.9 points.
On longitudinal questions, plain RAG scores 22.6% against the agent's 32.2%, so the loop adds 9.6 points.
The loop's gain is coverage: repeated querying lifts the retrieval ceiling, most on longitudinal, but longitudinal still caps around 44%.

## In short

The factual-versus-longitudinal gap, 87% against 32%, is dominantly a retrieval problem: evidence for barely 44% of what a trajectory answer must say is ever retrieved.
The ReAct loop and its repeated querying lift that ceiling from about 28% to about 44%, but neither a better ranker nor a wider context window gets past it.
The agent's reasoning is not the bottleneck.
The next thing worth building is retrieval that can surface evidence spread thinly across time, which is a different problem from making the agent smarter.

## Code companion

The [bounded-deep-research repo](https://github.com/chanys/bounded-deep-research) has the evaluation code under `eval/`: the claim and nugget extraction, the judge, the calibration, and both ablations.
The frozen-agent provenance described in the [first article](/posts/the-agent-is-the-easy-part/index.qmd) (each run stamped with its recipe version and git SHA) is what let one agent be held fixed and scored against every ablation here.
